title: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next
description: Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Tru
body: Republicans descended on Dallas this week to turn their midterm prospects around, hoping an unprecedented convention dominated by President Donald Trump would energise voters ahead of the November election.Many left the gathering - billed ahead of time by supporters as a "Trump-a-palooza" political fest - just as worried about the party's chances in 2026, and wondering what the Republicans' future will look like after the president leaves office.Vice-President JD Vance, who is widely viewed as a top contender to succeed Trump, offered his a party a glimpse of its potential future during his keynote address on Thursday night."We've got to take care of business this November," Vance told the crowds. "Then we'll worry about what comes next."His speech was interrupted at one point by chants of "48" - a nod to Trump's successor, who will become the 48th US president if they win in 2028. Vance let the chant linger briefly before waving it away.Over the two-day event, party activists were split on the wisdom of holding a midterm convention featuring a president who has record low approval ratings, and amid public frustration over the economy and war with Iran."I think it will make a difference. If anything it allows us to test the [campaign] message in front of a large audience," Jeff Ryer, the Virginia Republican Party chairman, told the BBC.Others said the president's rambling, nearly two-hour convention speech on Wednesday wouldn't sway voters weighing whether to keep Republicans in power in Congress.Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance to retake control of the House and the Senate is also in play, though viewed as more of a long shot for the party."Do I wish Trump gave a shorter speech? Sure, but that's not who he is," said one Republican operative, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to offer a blunt view of Trump's convention appearance.The source added that Trump's plea for voters to pretend as if he's on the ballot would fall flat."I don't think saying 'pretend I'm on the ballot' will work. He's not," the person said.The convention offered a stark reminder that the Trump era is heading toward its final chapter.Trump's presence loomed over the proceedings at the American Airlines Center in downtown Dallas.Republican House and Senate candidates lavished the president with praise in speeches, and supporters showed up wearing the red Maga hats that have become synonymous with Trump's political movement.The gathering was just two days, but still had the look and feel of the traditional four-day conventions staged by both parties in presidential election years. Organisers distributed signs and unleashed a balloon drop at the end as live music blared.Republicans had never held a midterm convention before.Vikki Consiglio, a party activist from Georgia, said it showcased Trump's ability to shake up political norms and capture the nation's attention.Evidence of that came when Trump pledged in his speech to make a payment of $5,000 to all American adults if Republicans retained control of Congress."He's a visionary. This whole convention is nothing but a vision," Consiglio said.But even as convention goers cheered Trump on, many seemed eager to discuss the 2028 presidential election."I'm very concerned about the next 10, 15, 20 years. I'm absolutely thinking about the future of the party," said Aiden Buzzetti, the president of The Bull Moose Project, a pro-Trump group.Buzzetti, who is 26, credited Trump with reshaping Republican politics, but said at the same time he was looking forward to a "new generation of conservative leaders."In interviews with the BBC, attendees at the convention most often mentioned Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio as the top contenders to replace Trump."Trump needs to pass the torch. We need to look forward," said Sandy Money, a Republican from Arizona who attended the convention. "I love Vance. But Rubio is my choice" if he runs in 2028, she said.Trump has openly mused about Rubio and Vance's chances to succeed him.But Vance and Rubio have deflected speculation about their political futures.Rubio was on a diplomatic trip to Ecuador during the convention, so he wasn't among the small handful of cabinet officials who attended the festivities in Dallas.The Trump administration has delivered "a great record of achievement," Vance argued, including improving the economy, strengthening border security and lowering the cost of prescription drugs.Vance said the contrast was clear with a Democratic Party that he argued had shifted radically to the left and turned into the "party of crazy". The vice-president also made a direct appeal to undecided voters, saying he wanted to win over "the people who are still making up their minds".Never one to cede the spotlight, Trump returned to the stage on Thursday night after Vance to round off the convention.For the president, the question of his successor was overshadowed by more immediate concerns."You know what happens if you don't vote?" he asked the gathered crowd. "You go to hell."

schema.headline: As Trump dominates convention, some Republicans quietly ask who comes next

title: Yemen's Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
description: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha
body: Yemen's Houthis have seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources and witnesses say.Mokha's capture leaves the Iran-backed group only 75km (46 miles) away from the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to a trade route that links Asia and Europe.The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia, which has relied on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.Mokha residents said Houthi fighters moved into the city after fierce clashes with pro-government forces on Wednesday night, prompting many families to flee their homes."The takeover came without warning. Panic spread throughout the area, forcing people to flee amid distressing scenes of injured people lying in the streets with no-one there to help them," one man told BBC Arabic's Middle East Lifeline programme.Another man said that Houthi fighters were patrolling the streets of Mokha on Thursday, while government offices and shops were closed."At the moment, we don't know what Ansar Allah will do," he added, using the group's formal name. "Everyone is afraid for their safety."Many displaced families are heading east towards the city of Aden, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based."We fled with our children and kept running. We have no bedding, no home, nothing with us. Everything was destroyed within an hour. They didn't even give us a chance or warn us beforehand," one woman told BBC Arabic."We are women with no means of defending ourselves, and we have innocent children with us."There was no immediate confirmation of Mokha's capture from the Houthis.But the group's Supreme Political Council said in a statement on Thursday that clashes had "ceased in the western coast districts after the expulsion of Saudi enemy mobilisations", according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.Tarek Salah, leader of the pro-government National Resistance Forces, also said he had moved his command centre on the west coast to a "safe location".He added that his forces had paid "a heavy price in recent days in the face of a Houthi offensive that was planned and supported by Iran".A Yemeni military source told AFP news agency that Houthi fighters had also seized Zuqar Island in the Red Sea, about 80km north-west of Mokha, after launching a barrage of rockets and a ground assault using boats.Meanwhile, the head of the Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, urged Arab states and other countries to help protect Yemen's coasts and restore state control.The Houthis' Supreme Political Council asserted its "right to defend [Yemen's] sovereignty and territorial waters while simultaneously reassuring the international community that navigation in the Red Sea remains safe".However, the Houthi-run humanitarian operations co-ordination centre also stressed that the embargo on Saudi ships remained in place.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said Saudi warplanes carried out 64 strikes across the western provinces of Taiz, Hudaydah, Marib and Jawf over the previous 24 hours.There was no immediate comment from the Saudi military.However, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday evening that it would respond to a series of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the south-western Saudi cities of Khamis Mushait, Abha and Jazan.On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on territory they control in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province on Monday that they said killed at least 23 civilians.The Saudi-led coalition has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

schema.headline: Yemen's Houthis seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha

title: Newcastle: Lewis Hall signs new contract until 2031
description: Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall has signed a new contract with the club that runs until 2031.The left-back, who has been the subject of interest
body: Newcastle United defender Lewis Hall has signed a new contract with the club that runs until 2031.The left-back, who has been the subject of interest from Manchester United, has agreed a two-year extension to his original deal.Hall said it was a "really proud moment" to extend his stay as a boyhood supporter of the club."It's an absolute pleasure to play for this club and to represent the supporters," he said. "I know how much it means to them."To be able to bring joy to their faces, it's a big thing for me. I obviously have a family connection with the club, which is incredibly important to us all. "One of the main reasons I play is to make my family proud, and I know how much it means to them to watch me playing for Newcastle United. "It's a really good place to be. It's really pleasing with how we've started the season, especially with the new gaffer [Matthias Jaissle] and coaching staff coming in, and I think we can go on to achieve really big things."Hall, 22, has made 106 appearances for Newcastle since joining the club from Chelsea in 2023.Jaissle said the defender is a "very important player for us and for what we are building here"."His mentality is exactly what you want in a young player," he said. "He wants to learn every day and he wants to be better in every match."Lewis covers ground in a way that few players can. He defends with maturity and intelligence, and his technical level means he can support the team higher up the pitch. "What excites me most is that I believe the best is still to come from Lewis. He has a lot of room to develop, and I am looking forward to working with him as he grows with us."This has been a busy summer at Newcastle - both in terms of ins and outs - but tying Hall down is a particularly significant move. It was just last month that Jaissle replied "no chance" when Manchester United legend Peter Schmeichel informed him that his former side were looking at Hall.This deal further strengthens the club's position.It also rewards Hall for his development since he arrived from Chelsea as a raw left-back three years ago.Hall needs to continue to work on the defensive side of his game but, on his day, he has proved he is capable of even keeping Barcelona star Lamine Yamal quiet from open play in the Champions League.He has been a real outlet going forward for Newcastle, too, and has already set up two goals this season.That should not come as a huge surprise.Of those full-backs to play a minimum of 900 minutes across the Premier League last season, Hall led the way for high-speed runs and underlapping runs per game. He also ranked in the top three for dribbles completed per match.It feels like there is a lot more to come from him as he looks to get back into the England squad after missing out on the World Cup.

schema.headline: Newcastle: Lewis Hall signs new contract until 2031

title: Philippine rescuers board burning ferry 40 hours after blaze began
description: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said."The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the shi
body: They finally got on at about 11:30 local time (03:30 GMT) on Friday, the coast guard said."The biggest challenge for us really is to penetrate the ship [as] there is still a visible, thick smoke," the coastguard's spokeswoman Noemie Cayabyab told the BBC earlier."No matter how we try to push through, high temperatures and toxic smoke remain a severe risk to our personnel," she told local media earlier.Smoke resulting from incomplete burning contains dense, lethal concentrations of carbon monoxide. Earlier, authorities reported that 86 were still unaccounted for, but as of Friday morning, the figure stood at 84 – two passengers whose names were on the ship's manifest did not go onboard, authorities say.Rescuers have widened their search area, Cayabyab says, adding that the coastguard has deployed one of its largest ships and done radio broadcasts to vessels in the area. The search teams are also accompanied by divers and nurses.A local diver in Coron told the BBC on Friday that he and his team were on standby to help out and awaiting instructions from the coast guard.The coast guard also conducted an aerial survey of waters near the disaster site. The plan is to resume firefighting efforts, first from the cargo hold of the ferry, which is the compartment where containers and or goods are stored, Cayabyab said. Earlier, the coastguard said preliminary interviews with the survivors suggest that was where the fire started. Some passengers were not wearing life vests, they noted.A survivor who was hauled to safety on a rescue boat had described the frantic cries on board the passenger-cargo vessel when the fire erupted on Wednesday evening.Roland Lerma recalled falling while scrambling to get off the burning boat."When I was on the floor, people were trampling me," the 30-year-old told the BBC.He started crawling until he could find his footing again, before leaping off the vessel into the sea. Lerma said he saw children who had also jumped in the water, though he could not make out their faces in the dark."It was cold [in the sea] If the rescue had been delayed, I would definitely have died," he said.The ferry, which set off from Manila, was nearing its destination at the tourist hotspot of Coron, in the province of Palawan, when it caught fire.The Philippines' maritime authority is investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident.The ferry, built in 2002, held valid safety certificates and passed an enforcement inspection in March, but investigators are looking into potential manifest discrepancies, cargo loading integrity, and crew emergency response protocols, the Palawan Daily reported.Atienza Interisland Ferries, the vessel's operator, has pledged full cooperation with the inquiry."Our hearts remain with the affected families, and we will not rest until all individuals are accounted for," the company said in a statement on Thursday.

schema.headline: Philippine rescuers board burning ferry 40 hours after blaze began

title: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina beats Coco Gauff to set up Aryna Sabalenka final
description: Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina produced a gritty comeback against Coco Gauff to reach the US Open final, in which she will face Aryna Saba
body: Soon-to-be world number one Elena Rybakina produced a gritty comeback against Coco Gauff to reach the US Open final, in which she will face Aryna Sabalenka in a blockbuster showdown between the tournament's top two seeds.Rybakina is guaranteed to end Sabalenka's 99-week reign as world number one and will replace the Belarusian at the top when the rankings are updated on Monday.But the Kazakh second seed could rub more salt in Sabalenka's wounds if she can deny the top seed a third successive US Open title in Saturday's showpiece.Sabalenka sent a warning to her rivals as she overpowered home hope Jessica Pegula 7-5 6-2 to keep alive her bid to become the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three times in a row.Rybakina will stand in her way after she fought back to beat American fourth seed Gauff 3-6 6-4 6-4 and silence the partisan crowd."I took a deep breath and just told myself I needed to fight and show good tennis," Rybakina said.The 27-year-old is chasing her third Grand Slam title after winning Wimbledon in 2022 and beating Sabalenka in January's Australian Open final.It will be the first time the top two women's seeds have contested a US Open final since Serena Williams beat Victoria Azarenka in the 2013 showpiece.Sabalenka has not been beaten in New York since losing the 2023 final to Gauff, but there were doubts over her title defence following a poor run-up to the tournament.After a strong start to the season and winning the 'Sunshine Double' at Indian Wells and Miami in March, Sabalenka suffered a quarter-final defeat at Roland Garros and a fourth-round exit at Wimbledon.However, she has found her form again, dropping just one set en route to the final."I was super desperate," Sabalenka said after her win over Pegula."It feels for me, talking about Grand Slams, like a last push of the season. "I wanted it badly to go to the finals, and of course, I want to go all the way."In a tense opening set, Sabalenka bristled with frustration early on as unforced errors crept into her game while Pegula settled quickly and struck the ball cleanly.But eventually the four-time major singles winner found her rhythm and, after striking decisively at 6-5 to take the first set, she cranked up the power.Pegula looked helpless as Sabalenka raced through the second set, with the Belarusian pounding 29 winners to her 12.The victory meant Sabalenka broke the Open era record for the most Grand Slam hard-court finals in a row, with the 28-year-old reaching every major final on her favoured surface since the 2023 Australian Open.For 32-year-old Pegula - the only semi-finalist without a Grand Slam title - it is yet another US Open defeat by long-time rival Sabalenka.Sabalenka denied the third seed a maiden major in the 2024 final, while she also got the better of her in last year's semi-finals - although Pegula had won their most recent meeting in June's Berlin Open."I do think she probably would have beaten 99% of people," Pegula said."Probably the best match she's played this year."Rybakina's ascent to the top of the world rankings is already assured but she has made it clear that for all the prestige of being number one, winning titles is what she really cares about."It's just a number right now, my goal is to win the tournaments which I play," the 27-year-old said before her semi-final.A three-set victory over Gauff showed all of Rybakina's resilience and ability to absorb a setback - coming from a set down and then being broken when serving for the match - before striking back.But for much of the match, she was well short of her destructive best."I definitely need to step my game up [in the final], serve better than today, stay aggressive and really go for my shots," the two-time major winner added.The prospect of a final between the top two seeds is tantalising enough but that it is the outgoing number one taking on her successor makes it all the more mouth-watering.While Sabalenka holds the edge in the head-to-head with 10 wins in 17 meetings, including beating Rybakina in the semi-finals in Miami and the final at Indian Wells this year, the Kazakh came out on top when they met in January's Australian Open final.Sabalenka led 3-0 in the deciding set in Melbourne but eventually fell to a third defeat in her past four Grand Slam finals.Meanwhile, Rybakina's only loss in three previous major finals was to Sabalenka in Australia in 2023.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Elena Rybakina beats Coco Gauff to set up Aryna Sabalenka final

title: World Athletics Ultimate Championship: Everything you need to know about new global competition
description: One trophy, no medals. Ten million dollars. A red carpet. A black infield. Noah Lyles as MC. Armand Duplantis singing before eyeing another world reco
body: One trophy, no medals. Ten million dollars. A red carpet. A black infield. Noah Lyles as MC. Armand Duplantis singing before eyeing another world record.This athletics season was set to be the first since the pandemic which did not culminate in an Olympic Games or World Championships.To bridge that gap, the sport's governing body has devised a new competition.Introducing: The World Athletics Ultimate Championship.Across three days of competition in Budapest, live on the BBC from 11-13 September, the world's top athletes will compete for record prize money and a new title.A new event pitching the best against the best, with increased financial commitments. You may be thinking: 'Haven't we been here before?'Last year, Michael Johnson's inaugural Grand Slam Track league attempted to maintain focus on the sport following Paris 2024 while offering lucrative prize money, but ended after encountering serious financial issues.This innovative, biennial format is bankrolled by World Athletics - and president Sebastian Coe has said he hopes to use it as an "incubator for change" which will shape the future of the sport's established World Championships.So, how does the Ultimate Championship work, what do the athletes think, and is it needed? Here is everything you need to know.The sport has long grappled with the issue of retaining the attention and excitement it generates at the Olympics throughout those four-year cycles. Because of the disruption caused by the pandemic, and subsequent postponement of the Tokyo 2020 Games, each of the past five years have provided a pinnacle event which gathered the biggest stars in front of a global audience.For many top British athletes, a 2026 season centred around a Commonwealth Games and European Championship on home soil would probably have finished at the Diamond League Final.Coe and World Athletics have planned for three years to fill that perceived void."It is an attempt to just start experimenting a bit and innovating, with an event that will determine who really is the best of the best," Coe told BBC Sport."There's no guarantee we're going get everything right, and no guarantee that everything is going to work. In two years, we might look at a slightly different format. "I also want to be able to put some of the things we're doing into the World Championship format. We have a responsibility to try and engage new young audiences."The Ultimate features a condensed three-night schedule, held as three-hour sessions.It is reserved for reigning Olympic, world and Diamond League champions, plus athletes who have qualified by world ranking.However, a few star names who did not qualify have been granted exceptional invitations, including Great Britain's Josh Kerr and Norwegian rival Jakob Ingebrigtsen into the men's 1500m.There will be a total of 28 finals, including straight finals in all field events and both the 1500m and the 5,000m. The 800m and shorter distances will have semi-finals.Not every discipline has been included, however. World Athletics says those decisions were taken based on the popularity of each event and data it gathered on viewer behaviour, including sweat response and pulse rate.As a result, long distance events such as the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, and field events such as the shot put and discus, have been left out.World Athletics is providing "the richest prize pot in the history of the sport" with a total of $10m (£7.4m) to be won.Each individual event winner will pocket $150,000 (£110,000) - more than double the offering at last year's World Championships - with $75,000 (£55,000) for the runner-up and $40,000 (£29,500) for third.Many of the sport's biggest names have voiced their support for athletics' new global event.Pole vault world record holder Duplantis was named as the inaugural 'Ultimate Star' last summer and has collaborated on the official anthem for the championship, Gold, which he has written and performed."It's super exciting. I think it was time to try something new and innovate within athletics," Duplantis said."It's tough for athletes when we have years without a championship. I think this fills the gap perfectly, you want to have some sort of climax to build towards."Kerr, set for a first race against rival Ingebrigtsen for two years, said the substantial increase in prize money showed how "serious" World Athletics are about the event. However, while the 2023 world champion agrees that a global championship was needed, he accepts there is "probably going to be some confusion from the outside world about what this is"."If that's what they're willing to put forward in prize money, it means that they're willing to put that effort into marketing and media," said Kerr."We're seeing progress. Obviously, $150,000 is a lot of money. It's not as much as other big sports, but they've earned that through years of pushing their marketing."But not everyone is convinced.Hurdles star Karsten Warholm has voiced his concern regarding the impact on the calendar, describing this year's late-season schedule as "chaos"."I think the Diamond League is a fantastic concept that should be cultivated. It will take a long time before people understand what an Ultimate Champion is," Warholm told Norwegian media outlet VG."It's pretty much the same athletes who participate but there could be two different winners at the Diamond League final and the Ultimate Championship."In terms of storytelling, it's going to be difficult. I don't think even athletics people are keeping up."There is also the matter of the excluded athletes and events.World triple jump champion Pedro Pichardo responded on social media to the decision to exclude his discipline: "I really don't understand what your problem is, and even less so making this decision without any explanation."This isn't track and field and it's not good for our sport."After ending her season with victory in the Diamond League Final, world shot put champion Chase Jackson told Citius Mag: "My body is saying 'yes' but my pockets are saying 'why the hell am I not at the Ultimate?' "How [do] you have track and field and just skip events? How does that make any sense?"

schema.headline: World Athletics Ultimate Championship: Everything you need to know about new global competition

title: I asked my husband to pay into my pension when we had a child - here's why
description: When Molly and Taylor Haylett started their family, they hadn't really planned for what it would mean financially."Our first child surprised us, so we
body: When Molly and Taylor Haylett started their family, they hadn't really planned for what it would mean financially."Our first child surprised us, so we weren't prepared for it," says Molly, 30, a financial adviser from Essex.Molly and Taylor, who's a train driver, were earning similar amounts, but once Molly spent more time at home with their baby, the balance changed."Taylor's career propelled and mine took a step back," she says. "There's an unintended impact on the person who spends more time at home with the kids."One of the things the couple decided to do was have Taylor contribute to Molly's pension while she was off work."We were looking after both our futures, not just Taylor's," Molly says.It is something she thinks far more couples should discuss before having children.Research by Octopus Money found more than a third of parents reduced or paused pension contributions during parental leave, while 63% did not know their partner could contribute on their behalf.A partner can make what is known as a third-party pension contribution. For someone with no or low earnings, up to £2,880 can be paid in each tax year, with basic-rate tax relief increasing that to £3,600.For someone still earning, their partner can also contribute, subject to the recipient's pension limits.Katie Guild, co-founder of financial community Nugget Savings, says the pension gap can begin during maternity leave because an employee's own contributions can fall as their pay drops, and contributions may stop altogether during periods of unpaid leave.She says couples should consider whether the partner continuing to work could help make up some of that shortfall.Before having a baby, she recommends working through a few key questions:Guild says these conversations are easier before a baby arrives than when parents are sleep-deprived and adjusting to life with a newborn.Molly and Taylor now have two children, aged two and five, and say they were much more prepared the second time around and stopped thinking about household costs as something that always needed to be divided exactly in half.The couple, who each earn around £60,000, have their own bank accounts alongside a joint account for bills, but are flexible with the amount each contributes when their circumstances change.During Molly's maternity leave, for example, they adjusted the split and she's found it helpful to "view finances as a household".The couple say they are teaching their children about money from an early age.They set pensions up for both kids when they were born and have been paying into them through a monthly direct debit.Molly explains: "It's like a gift for the future as they can't touch that money until they're in their 60s and we won't be there to see that."They also use Junior ISAs, although Molly points out that once the children are old enough, the money becomes theirs to spend "and if they want to, they can take that money and blow it in Ibiza".Taylor says their five-year-old is given small jobs to earn a couple of pounds, rather than simply being bought everything she asks for. They are also beginning to introduce the idea of saving by telling her that she can spend a pound now or hold on to it and potentially have more later.Guild says couples should check what support they can receive, including funded childcare hours, external and Tax-Free Childcare, external.She adds that conversations about money should not stop once parental leave begins and when the baby arrives she advises couples should:

title: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out
description: Image source, PA MediaByHenry ZeffmanChief political correspondentAt the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham look
body: Image source, PA MediaByHenry ZeffmanChief political correspondentAt the start of summer, in the pillared room in 10 Downing Street, Andy Burnham looked out at his new special advisers, the few dozen political officials tasked with driving hundreds of thousands of civil servants to deliver his government's agenda.Some had been with him in Manchester or Makerfield. Others had spent the past few months trying everything to prevent his hostile takeover of Sir Keir Starmer's government - and the new prime minister showed he was aware of it, going out of his way to praise those who had stayed on, for their efforts in the preceding years.At that meeting, Burnham's team mapped out four key moments in the coming months.First, the return to Parliament in September, when Burnham and other leading ministers would make their first statements to MPs. Second, Labour's annual conference at the end of September - Burnham's first as leader. Third, the Budget, taking place on 28 October. And fourth, the 10-year plan for Britain which Burnham intends to unveil in November.As MPs prepare to leave Parliament on Tuesday for almost a month and party conference season gets underway, the first phase of that route map is almost complete - enough for figures at all levels of the Labour Party to begin answering some questions about the shape of this new government.Most importantly, perhaps, how new actually is it? Does Burnham represent continuity or change?That question is especially relevant because those Labour MPs who pushed for Sir Keir to be replaced always fell into two broad camps: those who wanted a change of style and emphasis but continuity in policy, and those who wanted a major shift in policy. Both groups saw what they wanted in Burnham.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Andy Burnham speaks during his first Cabinet meeting since becoming prime ministerGoing by the words of the new prime minister himself, he represents a profound break with the past, and not only the immediate past. In his first speech as Labour leader in July, Burnham described his ascendancy as "the most significant change moment in our politics for 40 years". That is the timeframe he has returned to again and again, signalling not just a desire to reverse issues he believes stem from the Thatcher era but also to break with aspects of the Labour governments since then, including his immediate predecessor's.Some in government are already quietly questioning, though, whether the ambition of that rhetoric can be squared with the early signals emerging from the Treasury under the new Chancellor John Healey.In interviews over recent weeks, and especially in his first major speech on Monday, Healey has said he will stick to Rachel Reeves's commitments not to increase the main rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT, as well as her rules on government borrowing.In the speech, he promised to "control public spending", and hailed Reeves for beginning to "recover Britain's fiscal discipline".It led to opposition parties labelling Healey a continuity chancellor. A similar critique is being voiced among some of his government colleagues.Most are more generous for now, arguing that Healey's first imperative - especially at a time of turmoil in the global bond markets - is reassurance, and that the Budget is the moment for him to show how he plans to substantiate Burnham's rhetoric. Even one official sympathetic on that point, though, asks: "Why did he do a big speech before he has something to say?"Those close to Healey argue that his emphasis this week on securing the economic growth which has eluded successive governments by spreading wealth around the country is a clear difference from Reeves. And finding ways to boost regional growth has been one of Healey's major causes since he was a junior minister at the Treasury more than 20 years ago - long before it was at the heart of Burnham's political personality.There is no question, though, that this week the minister who most starkly signalled change from the previous government was a man who coveted Healey's job - Ed Miliband, who was instead appointed foreign secretary.In announcing new sanctions on Israel over illegal settlements in the West Bank, Miliband explicitly cast the policy as a break from Sir Keir's approach, telling MPs: "We should have acted earlier, and it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation."On the other hand, acting alongside Canada and France in announcing the sanctions represented - in form if not substance  - continuity with the previous government, the three countries having moved together to recognise the state of Palestine a year ago.The sanctions announcement was received with near-universal warmth from Labour MPs, itself a marker of change from the Starmer government.It was also seen as a sign of the ability of Miliband in particular, but this government in general, to drive its agenda through the civil service machine. "There is a much clearer sense now from No 10 of what they want," one official who worked under Sir Keir as well as Burnham says. "Before there was a bit too much of 'let us know your ideas for what we should do', now it's 'this is what the PM wants, give us options to deliver it'."That is a culture shift which Burnham sought to drill into his cabinet at their weekly meeting on Tuesday, still only their third such meeting. According to one present, the prime minister said: "We need to be on the front foot. We need to be bolder. Let's get on and do things. It's about deeds not words."Image caption, Burnham has called for "growth in every postcode", and the establishment of No 10 North is a key part of that agendaPerhaps the most significant way in which Burnham is trying to make boldness easier for his ministers is by encouraging them to press ahead with policies when there is a risk they will face a serious legal challenge. The new attorney general, Ellie Reeves, has pared back rules introduced under Sir Keir which some ministers believed forced them to be over-cautious about legal risk, thereby slowing down or blocking new policies altogether.Louise Haigh, Burnham's deputy, has vowed to "strip out needless bureaucracy" from government more generally, citing an example of there being three public consultations between 2019 and 2023 on whether to microchip cats. "If we can't microchip cats without getting tied up in red tape, it should come as no surprise the public is losing faith that governments can get things done," she said.As Burnham moves into the next phase of his autumn, there is a recognition from some around him that he will need to produce some more significant policies to underpin his rhetoric. Those in government familiar with early work on fleshing out his commitment to "public control" of essential services insist the direction of travel is truly radical. Haigh is responsible for this, chairing a taskforce on how to reverse "over-privatisation" specifically of housing, water, energy and transport.Burnham may offer more details on these policies at Labour's conference, while he is likely to wait until after then to show his hand on whether he wants continuity or change when it comes to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's reforms to the legal immigration system - a much more divisive issue among Labour MPs.And whatever their differences on policy, Labour MPs are united on one thing. The fundamental reason they installed a new prime minister was because many of them believed that continuing on the same path meant losing the next general election. For them, a long-term improvement in Labour's poll ratings would be the most important change of them all.

schema.headline: Henry Zeffman: How Burnham got ready to govern with four key moments mapped out

title: Angela Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul in England
description: Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challe
body: Angela Rayner has defended her decision to pause plans to redraw local council boundaries, saying she wanted to ensure they would survive legal challenge.The local government secretary also told the BBC she wanted to be "clear-eyed" about what the planned shake-up in 16 areas of England was likely to achieve.It comes after earlier this week she abandoned proposals in four other areas, in the face of legal threats from Reform and Conservative-led authorities.The surprise announcement on Monday has thrown the reorganisation plans into doubt, and drawn criticism from local leaders preparing for the changes.Councils in affected areas have been drawing up proposals and consulting with residents since the reorganisation was announced in late 2024, in a process that is already thought to have cost millions of pounds. Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson podcast, Rayner conceded the decision to press pause had been "difficult" and she understood local authorities had put a "lot of time and effort" into their plans.But she added she wanted to have "all the information" about the proposals before going ahead with them, after her reappointment to her cabinet role under Andy Burnham, ten months after her resignation last year."I got the legal advice and I hadn't had the time to review and to go through all of that, and court cases were looming," she told the podcast."If I'm making a decision that is highly likely to be in legal challenge, I want to make sure I've dotted my i's and crossed my t's," she added.Rayner also said she wanted was "really clear-eyed on where we were going" with the plans, after Burnham had asked her to look again at the blueprints, which were announced by her predecessor Steve Reed.In her announcement on Monday, Rayner said she was withdrawing plans to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.Those proposals, announced in March, were already subject to legal challenges from Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk, and the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire, which were lodged over the summer.She also said she wanted to review plans for 16 other areas, including 14 announced by Reed days before Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister and reappointed her to her old role.Some councils affected by those plans, including Kent and Leicestershire, had threatened similar bids to challenge the lawfulness of the decision-making process.The government has argued that the plans, which will abolish remaining two-tier areas in England where county and district councils share responsibility for services, would make local government more effective and cost efficient.However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.Others have also complained that the reorganisation could stymie or delay parallel efforts to merge councils into regional authorities led by mayors, which Burnham has cited as a key part of his economic plans.Elsewhere in her interview, Rayner said Labour under Sir Keir should have been quicker to recognise a Palestinian state, having promised to do so as a "contribution to a renewed peace process" at the last election.Starmer took the move in September last year, having spent much of the prior year  resisting pressure to do so from Labour MPs."It's always been Labour policy to recognise a Palestinian state, and it felt like we got there too late. It was something that should have been really clear," she said.She also denied that UK sanctions against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, announced on Tuesday, had been made to help Labour ahead of the forthcoming by-election in Holborn and St Pancras in central London.Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.Pointing to the fact that Western allies had also announced sanctions, she said: "The French and the Canadians are not going to be like 'oh well, we'll just signal something to help you with a local by-election in London'".Reflecting on her return to government, she said a "big difference" between Burnham and his predecessor in Downing Street was his inclination to tell "the story of why we're doing something" in government.She said both men shared "passion and the commitment" to deliver for Labour in office, but added: "Andy is probably more like me, in terms of [he] wears his heart on his sleeve". The interview with Angela Rayner will be broadcast on BBC2 at 12:30 BST on Friday 11 September, and 17:30 BST on Saturday 12 September.

schema.headline: Angela Rayner defends pause to local council overhaul in England

title: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons
description: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological
body: Anthropic says it has identified and disrupted attempts to use its AI model for "malicious activity" which could support the development of biological weapons.The claim, made in the firm's recent threat intelligence report, is the latest in a growing series of warnings from AI researchers and industry insiders about the technology's potential risks to humanity.The warning has prompted calls to action, with US Senator Bernie Sanders demanding a pause on advanced AI development and a ban on artificial superintelligence.President Donald Trump has so far rejected such fears, saying on Thursday he was concerned "if we don't win AI, we're going to be put in a very bad position".The company published its latest threat intelligence report, external on Thursday. Other AI firms publish similar reports.This includes Google, who wrote on Tuesday, external a person had attempted to use its AI tool Gemini to "complete, step-by-step technical guide for synthesizing weaponised biological agents".Anthropic's AI model Claude was also used in a Russia-linked cyber espionage campaign and by an Iranian propaganda institution, according to Anthropic's report.The cases of concern detected over the past eight months ranged from fake dating apps and hotel Wifi scams, to surveillance built to identify dissidents.Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI firms of trying to replicate Claude's capabilities. The lengthy report lists cases in which suspected state-sponsored groups, criminals, spyware vendors, state propaganda institutions and politically motivated individuals misused its technology."Malicious use" of its Claude Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus models was disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026, it said.None of the misuse cases involved Claude Fable or the powerful Mythos-class models, with the exception of one instance of distillation - the process for training smaller AI models using larger, more expensive models.As well as detecting the use of its models for cyber and influence operations, surveillance, scams and fraud and weapon development, Anthropic said it had blocked scientists who used its AI in ways that could support biological weapons development.The report highlighted "five case studies of actors using our models in ways that could support biological weapons development".Biological misuse, it said, is "one of the most serious risks of frontier AI model". Without the correct safeguards, such capabilities "could have catastrophic consequences", Anthropic said."The same information that can be used to develop a biological weapon could also be used to develop, for example, a vaccine or a cure for a disease," Anthropic said.Jacob Klein, the head of threat intelligence at Anthropic, told the New York Times, external it was "an incredibly nuanced situation"."You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" he said.The report also noted six cases where Claude was used "to develop software for conventional weapons, including firearms, missiles, armed drones, bombs, and other munitions, as well as the targeting and control systems that operate them".The report indicated that cybercriminals and state-backed hackers have increasingly used its technology to assist their operations.Hacking group ShinyHunters, as well as China-based labs, were among those named in the report.The report also said that a hacking group whose work is consistent with the Russia-based Midnight Blizzard allegedly used AI to build a system that automatically detected when its malware was flagged by security defences and rewrote code until it evaded detection.The California-based company said it had incorporated its findings into its processes "to better prevent, detect, and disrupt these activities in the future".Anthropic said it had shared intelligence with authorities and industry partners where appropriate.The report - the company's first this year - comes after a top safety researcher at Anthropic warned AI is advancing so quickly he believes there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.In an article published on 6 September, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki called for the industry to implement "voluntary slowdowns" until safeguards are set."I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence," Pachocki said, adding that OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, will continue its work on building safeguards, though broader interventions are required.The warning prompted an open letter to UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham calling for a new multinational treaty for the safe development of AI and a call for governments to collaborate about what a treaty based on the development of superintelligence should look like.In the US, Democratic lawmaker Bernie Sanders has introduced legislation to ban AI  superintelligence and temporarily pause advanced AI development."When scientists tell you there is a chance, a chance that it could have a cataclysmic impact on humanity, you've got be a moron not to say, slow it down," he said on Thursday on BBC's Newsnight.With additional reporting from Osmond Chia.

schema.headline: Anthropic blocks possible attempt to use AI to make biological weapons

title: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure
description: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's father
body: For 25 years, the only physical trace Juliette Scauso has had from the last day of her father's life is his mangled firefighter helmet.Scauso's father, Dennis - part of a New York City Fire Department (FDNY) hazmat unit for 12 years -  initially was not scheduled to work on 11 September, 2001, but switched shifts for the overtime pay.The Long Island father of four was likely in the South Tower of the World Trade Center when it collapsed, the Scauso family was told. The helmet with his badge number was found months later."I've spent essentially my entire life knowing my father died, and learning to live with the fact that we never recovered him," said Scauso, who was four when he died.Dennis Scauso is one of more than 1,000 people killed on September 11 in New York who have yet to be identified, according to New York City's Office of Chief Medical Examiner. Nearly 3,000 people died in the World Trade Center attacks that day.Last month, the city announced the identity of a previously unknown victim of the terrorist attacks - the 1,654th person - using a new technology called forensic investigative genetic genealogy - or FIGG."There is real promise in using this approach," said Angela Soler, director of forensic anthropology in the city's medical examiner office. "There's hope for more families to receive answers, and hopefully we'll be able to test more remains in the future using this technology as well."Since 9/11, Soler's office has sought to identify the remains of the 2,753 victims who died in the World Trade Center. So far, 60 percent of those killed have been identified."It's been one of the most complex identification efforts that I think anybody has ever really experienced," Soler said.Efforts to identify victims have been complicated by a number of factors.Human remains were damaged in the plane crashes and fires caused by jet fuel, meaning the office had only portions of victims for DNA samples, Soler said.Scauso added that because of the timing of the attacks, many firefighters were changing shifts, but some stayed to help, grabbing whatever extra gear they could find. This meant some first responders recovered were wearing uniforms with others' names, complicating identification.The World Trade Center site also had many more victims than the other 9/11 terrorist attack sites.The remains of five of the 184 people killed when American Airlines Flight 77 crashed into the Pentagon were never identified because of similar conditions. According to the National Park Service, enough remains were recovered to use DNA, dental records and fingerprints to identify all 40 victims aboard United Airlines flight 93, which crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.Remains from the World Trade Center have been packaged and sealed to help preserve DNA for testing in the years to come. Soon after the attacks, individuals were identified using fingerprints or dental records, but as time went on, when neither was available, the office turned to DNA. Officials were able to use new technology to extract DNA and retest the same remains."That's why all these years down the road, we're still getting new identifications, because we're just continuing to retest and retry with every new technology that becomes available," Soler said.DNA technology has helped the office identify 1,495 victims since 9/11 - some solely with DNA and others with multiple methods - according to the medical examiner's office.Last year, the city announced that with the help of DNA, 24 years later, it had identified three new victims - Ryan Fitzgerald, a 26-year-old currency trader, Babara Keating, a 72-year-old who was aboard American Airlines Flight 11 from Boston to Los Angeles, and a woman whose family kept her identity private.Soler said the new FIGG technology uses whole genome sequencing - which provides a way to read someone's entire genetic code. It means investigators can make more potential matches to family members who are more distant relatives of the victim. Once those matches are made, the New York Police Department helps find relatives who are closer to the victims.The medical examiner's office in New York still gets weekly calls from loved ones asking about someone whose remains were never recovered.Many have never been able to bury a loved one, but some families choose to leave the remains - once found - at a repository at the 9/11 memorial site in New York. The repository was built into the bedrock of the World Trade Center site and can only be accessed by medical examiner staff. A nearby private space, known as the reflection room, is available for families to mourn."That's where their loved one was in their last moments, and that's where they want them to stay", Soler said.Some don't want to be notified, perhaps because the confirmation is too painful, said Soler, who helps inform families.Scauso is one of those people. She knows people who, in recent years, got a call that a relative finally has been identified. The thought of being next on the list is scary for her family, who has worked hard to keep the memory of her father - a jack of all trades and a lover of jazz - alive."At this point, an identification wouldn't change the reality of his death. It wouldn't give me back my father, and I don't necessarily want to reopen something that has become part of the way I've learned to live and grieve," she said. "Especially 25 years later, it's going to open up the wounds again."But, Scauso said, the technology is important.Soler has seen the news provide a mix of both relief and sadness. "It's confirmation of something that they always knew to be true - they knew their loved one died on 9/11, but I think for many families, there's still that question in the back of their mind until the remains are formally identified," Soler said."Maybe they're reliving it a little bit more now, having this new identification. But at the same time, it closes one chapter of their journey after 9/11," she added.To Soler - and some of her current colleagues who also were on the ground during 9/11 - the work is deeply personal. Workers from their office arrived at Ground Zero after the planes hit the towers, and were there when the buildings collapsed.They are aware it is unlikely they will identify every victim of the New York attacks. In some instances, there may be no remains of a victim at all. Still, they have no plans to stop."As long as there's families looking for answers, we'll continue searching for them," she said.

schema.headline: New technology may bring more 9/11 victims' families closure

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Day that changed the world forever' and 'Mayors plot holiday tax'
description: Many of the papers lead on the government's plans to introduce a tourist tax in England. The Guardian describes it as "a hammer blow" for the hotel in
body: Many of the papers lead on the government's plans to introduce a tourist tax in England. The Guardian describes it as "a hammer blow" for the hotel industry., external But it says some regional mayors have welcomed the proposals. The Daily Mail says Andy Burnham has been accused of launching another raid on struggling families., external "Welfare party strikes again," it says on its front page. According to the Daily Telegraph, the founder of the pub chain, JD Wetherspoon, said the plans would likely lead to higher prices, external across the hospitality sector. The Sun says working people have been "whacked" and asks "what the hol, PM?"., externalThe Daily Mirror leads with the words of the assisted dying campaigner, Dame Esther Rantzen, who says her cancer has left her too frail now to travel to Dignitas, external. The headline is "It's too late for me". The Daily Star says the TV presenter is pleading with MPs to pass the assisted dying bill, external. A terminally ill mother interviewed in the Daily Express, external calls on ministers to "just pass the bill".The Metro leads on the 25th anniversary of the 11 September 2001 attacks. Its front page simply reads '9/11', external. "The day that changed the world," reads the i newspaper's front page - which features a picture of a firefighter standing in the rubble of the fallen towers., externalHousehold energy bills could increase by more than a £100 by the end of the decade, external, according to the front page of the Times. It says delays to new power lines -- needed to hit the government's clean power pledge - are to blame. A spokesperson for Neso, the government-owned body in charge of keeping Britain's lights on, said it was doing everything it could to keep costs down.The Sun says the crew of an RAF Chinook helicopter was seen landing in the grounds of a luxury hotel on the shores of Loch Lomond, external, before leaving with cakes and other treats. An RAF source said hotel staff unexpectedly provided food during the planned stop. The paper dubs the airmen "the royal eclair force".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Day that changed the world forever' and 'Mayors plot holiday tax'

title: Practical Magic 2's Maisie Williams: People long for simpler times
description: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot starsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are jo
body: People long for simpler times, say Practical Magic reboot starsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast of the sequel to portray the daughters of Sandra Bullock's character ByNaomi ClarkeBBC NewsbeatMix together a beloved film simmering for decades, a sprinkling of social media hype and a generous glug of star power and you just might conjure up the long-awaited sequel to Practical Magic. The 1998 fantasy romcom, starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witchy sisters Sally and Gillian Owens, received mixed reviews from critics when it was first released.But it's put a spell on a new generation discovering it online, with some now regarding the film as a cult classic and autumn staple.The demand for a follow-up by this new wave of fans helped convince Bullock and Kidman to reprise their roles nearly 30 years on, they say. "You never get the opportunity to do something where people really are asking you, 'please do it'," says Bullock. "It's usually us going to them."Actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams are joining the cast this time round to play Sally's daughters, Kylie and Antonia. Kissing Booth star King tells BBC Newsbeat she feels this desire for nostalgic content, which has become one of the defining forces within entertainment in recent years, has been influenced by "the world moving so fast".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Practical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic"I think with technology moving at the speed that it is, we're really missing the times when we were less reachable," she says."If we couldn't figure out something, we'd stare out the window until it came to us, and I think we're nostalgic for a time like that."  She feels this can also be a strength of cinema as it can help "make memories" and "feelings" for people that they can revisit by rewatching. The upcoming release comes at a time when reboots, reunions and remakes are dominating film and TV lists.Game of Thrones star Williams agrees the drive for nostalgic content feels like a "symptom of people longing for simpler times", but says she is "very grateful" that they have made a sequel and not a remake. "I do believe in pushing the story forwards and I do believe in telling new stories," she says."And I do believe stories can come back around and they can still be meaningful."But I am not the biggest fan of the remake because I think it's a shame to withhold ourselves from telling a new story." Image source, Warner Bros. PicturesImage caption, The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the 1998 film and continues into the sequelPractical Magic 2 sees the cast return to a world which is steeped in powerful ancestral magic with the characters once again confronting a family curse which condemns anyone who loves and is loved by an Owens woman to death.There are also nods to the original throughout, with bubbling family tension, dark romantic "witchcore" fashion and the iconic midnight margaritas.US acting stalwarts Dianne Wiest and Stockard Channing return to their roles for the follow-up, while Guardians of the Galaxy actor Lee Pace, Cobra Kai's Xolo Maridueña and House of the Dragon's Solly McLeod are new additions. Reviews so far have been mixed, with the Guardian describing it as a "nostalgia-bait return", external which is as "strange and messy as the first" but with "warm seasonal pleasures to be had".Meanwhile The Hollywood Reporter, external says the "slapdash" sequel "works better the less you look for any sense of logic, and the more you just lean into the transient joys of watching these actresses bounce off each other".Image source, Warner Bros. PicturesImage caption, Joey King says the idea of "being witchy" can be "empowering right now"Amid the scrutiny around the film, Williams admits joining the Practical Magic world was "a little bit overwhelming", but says the cast were "so supportive the whole time" and "welcomed us into the sisterhood".The bond of sisterhood is at the heart of the first film and continues in the sequel, but Bullock has recalled this was initially one of the criticisms of the original, external, with some branding it as "too witchy" with "too many women". With women's rights under pressure in some countries, Williams says it is a "challenging time" and she feels it's "so important in a time like this for women to be supporting one another"."We are in a time when young women are staying in education longer and women, before having children, are sometimes being paid more than their male counterparts, which I do find to be really exciting," she adds."But there's a lot of work to do."And this feeling of witches, symbiosis and power - I feel like there's something in that which can just push us forwards."Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Practical Magic 2's Maisie Williams: People long for simpler times

title: Your partner's snoring could be impacting your health
description: Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response. When it is disrupted, these systems can become less
body: Sleep also plays a role in regulating the brain systems involved in stress and emotional response. When it is disrupted, these systems can become less balanced, which may make you feel more irritable and less able to cope with stress.This is something Meg Warren, 29, experienced when her former partner's snoring would keep her up.She says: "Without fail, after a snoring-induced wake up I would feel on incredibly high alert."Meg, a charity media officer, would prod him throughout the night and try to coax him from his back to his side. She says she would wake up "feeling groggy and dazed, sometimes so much so that it would feel like a hangover".The snoring tested the relationship, with Meg explaining: "I always said if we lived together we'd have to have a spare bedroom for the nights of truly unbearable snoring."Simon says that broken sleep, caused by a partner's snoring, can lead to irritability, arguments, and - if it is decided that sleeping in separate rooms is needed - reduced intimacy.There are things that can be done, say both Simon and Johal. But first, it is important to distinguish whether your partner is simply snoring, or whether they have sleep apnoea."What you don't want to do is simply make someone quieter at night while potentially missing an underlying sleep-related breathing disorder," Simon says. Signs of sleep apnoea, a disorder that causes a person's breathing to repeatedly stop and start during sleep, include pauses in breathing, choking at night, waking frequently, and suffering from morning headaches. If this is what you are dealing with, you could be recommended a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine, or even surgical treatment in some cases, Simon explains.For simple snoring, Simon said that lifestyle changes can make a difference, such as losing weight, stopping smoking, reducing alcohol intake before bed, or changing your sleeping position - such as laying on your side rather than your back.You can also suggest to your partner that they see a GP, who will be able to advise further or refer you to a specialist. An expert might suggest treating nasal obstruction or allergies, if this is what is causing snoring, or wearing a custom mouthguard to gently push the lower jaw forward and keep the airway open.Johal says too many couples put up with snoring "for too long", which impacts their relationships and wellbeing."The key thing is that there is help out there, it's just tapping into it."

schema.headline: Your partner's snoring could be impacting your health
